lines.text: Ecuador killed its own money at 25,000 to $1.
lines.say: Ecuador killed its own money at twenty-five thousand to one dollar.

lines.text: In January 2000, it took 25,000 sucres to buy one US dollar. A year earlier, it took about 7,000.
lines.say: In January two thousand, it took twenty-five thousand sucres to buy one US dollar. A year earlier, it took about seven thousand.

lines.text: So Ecuador did something drastic. It stopped using its own currency and adopted America's dollar instead.
lines.say: So Ecuador did something drastic. It stopped using its own currency and adopted America's dollar instead.

lines.text: And it isn't alone. Panama has used the US dollar since 1904, and it has no central bank printing its own bills.
lines.say: And it isn't alone. Panama has used the US dollar since nineteen oh four, and it has no central bank printing its own bills.

lines.text: Here's the plan: Panama's century-old deal, Ecuador's fall, the pros and cons, and what it all means for regular people's wallets.
lines.say: Here's the plan: Panama's century-old deal, Ecuador's fall, the pros and cons, and what it all means for regular people's wallets.

lines.text: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.
lines.say: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.

lines.text: Chapter one: a borrowed dollar.
lines.say: Chapter one: a borrowed dollar.

lines.text: First, a definition. Dollarization means a country uses another country's money, usually the US dollar, as its own official currency.
lines.say: First, a definition. Dollarization means a country uses another country's money, usually the US dollar, as its own official currency.

lines.text: That's different from a peg. Hong Kong, which we covered in an earlier episode, keeps its own currency and fixes its price. A dollarized country drops its own notes entirely.
lines.say: That's different from a peg. Hong Kong, which we covered in an earlier episode, keeps its own currency and fixes its price. A dollarized country drops its own notes entirely.

lines.text: Panama's story starts in 1904, right after its independence. A monetary agreement with the US made the American dollar legal tender there.
lines.say: Panama's story starts in nineteen oh four, right after its independence. A monetary agreement with the US made the American dollar legal tender there.

lines.text: Panama's own unit, the balboa, is worth exactly one dollar. It exists only as coins, while US bills do the paper-money job.
lines.say: Panama's own unit, the balboa, is worth exactly one dollar. It exists only as coins, while US bills do the paper-money job.

lines.text: So when you pay for lunch in Panama City, you hand over the same greenbacks you'd use in Ohio.
lines.say: So when you pay for lunch in Panama City, you hand over the same greenbacks you'd use in Ohio.

lines.text: There was one strange exception. In October 1941, President Arnulfo Arias had Panama print its own balboa banknotes.
lines.say: There was one strange exception. In October nineteen forty-one, President Arnulfo Arias had Panama print its own balboa banknotes.

lines.text: About a week later, Arias was overthrown. The new government pulled the notes and burned the rest. Collectors call them the seven-day notes.
lines.say: About a week later, Arias was overthrown. The new government pulled the notes and burned the rest. Collectors call them the seven-day notes.

lines.text: Panama went straight back to the dollar, and it has stayed there ever since.
lines.say: Panama went straight back to the dollar, and it has stayed there ever since.

lines.text: That means Panama can't create dollars when it needs more. Every dollar has to come in from outside, through trade, investment, or borrowing.
lines.say: That means Panama can't create dollars when it needs more. Every dollar has to come in from outside, through trade, investment, or borrowing.

lines.text: Chapter two: Ecuador's meltdown.
lines.say: Chapter two: Ecuador's meltdown.

lines.text: Ecuador's road to the dollar was much rougher. In the late 1990s, it had its own currency, the sucre, and its own central bank.
lines.say: Ecuador's road to the dollar was much rougher. In the late nineteen nineties, it had its own currency, the sucre, and its own central bank.

lines.text: Then a lot went wrong at once. First, a deep recession hit the economy.
lines.say: Then a lot went wrong at once. First, a deep recession hit the economy.

lines.text: Second, banks started failing, one after another.
lines.say: Second, banks started failing, one after another.

lines.text: Third, the sucre itself collapsed.
lines.say: Third, the sucre itself collapsed.

lines.text: And fourth, the government defaulted on its debt.
lines.say: And fourth, the government defaulted on its debt.

lines.text: The IMF says the sucre fell 54% during 1998 alone.
lines.say: The I M F says the sucre fell fifty-four percent during nineteen ninety-eight alone.

lines.text: In February 1999, the central bank gave up defending its exchange-rate band and let the sucre float.
lines.say: In February nineteen ninety-nine, the central bank gave up defending its exchange-rate band and let the sucre float.

lines.text: Then, in March 1999, the government declared a bank holiday and froze people's deposits.
lines.say: Then, in March nineteen ninety-nine, the government declared a bank holiday and froze people's deposits.

lines.text: It was announced as a short freeze. According to Ecuador's El Comercio newspaper, it dragged on for months, and millions couldn't reach their savings.
lines.say: It was announced as a short freeze. According to Ecuador's El Comercio newspaper, it dragged on for months, and millions couldn't reach their savings.

lines.text: Meanwhile, the sucre kept sinking, from about 7,000 per dollar in January 1999 to 25,000 by January 2000.
lines.say: Meanwhile, the sucre kept sinking, from about seven thousand per dollar in January nineteen ninety-nine to twenty-five thousand by January two thousand.

lines.text: Here's an example. Say a family had 10 million sucres saved in January 1999.
lines.say: Here's an example. Say a family had ten million sucres saved in January nineteen ninety-nine.

lines.text: At about 7,000 per dollar, 10 million divided by 7,000 is about $1,429.
lines.say: At about seven thousand per dollar, ten million divided by seven thousand is about one thousand four hundred twenty-nine dollars.

lines.text: At 25,000 per dollar, the same 10 million sucres is worth just $400.
lines.say: At twenty-five thousand per dollar, the same ten million sucres is worth just four hundred dollars.

lines.text: Same pile of sucres, same bank. In dollar terms, about 72% of it was gone.
lines.say: Same pile of sucres, same bank. In dollar terms, about seventy-two percent of it was gone.

lines.text: And prices raced up. In 2000, consumer prices in Ecuador rose 96.1%, according to World Bank data.
lines.say: And prices raced up. In two thousand, consumer prices in Ecuador rose ninety-six point one percent, according to World Bank data.

lines.text: On average, prices in 2000 were nearly double their 1999 level.
lines.say: On average, prices in two thousand were nearly double their nineteen ninety-nine level.

lines.text: Many people simply left. El Comercio calls it one of the largest emigration waves in Ecuador's history, mainly to the US and Europe.
lines.say: Many people simply left. El Comercio calls it one of the largest emigration waves in Ecuador's history, mainly to the US and Europe.

lines.text: Then came the big decision. On January 9, 2000, President Jamil Mahuad announced that Ecuador would adopt the US dollar.
lines.say: Then came the big decision. On January ninth, two thousand, President Jamil Mahuad announced that Ecuador would adopt the US dollar.

lines.text: Less than two weeks later, on January 21, Mahuad was pushed out of office in a short-lived coup.
lines.say: Less than two weeks later, on January twenty-first, Mahuad was pushed out of office in a short-lived coup.

lines.text: His vice president, Gustavo Noboa, took over, and he kept the dollar plan going.
lines.say: His vice president, Gustavo Noboa, took over, and he kept the dollar plan going.

lines.text: Congress passed the law in late February, and it took effect on March 13, 2000, locking in 25,000 sucres per dollar.
lines.say: Congress passed the law in late February, and it took effect on March thirteenth, two thousand, locking in twenty-five thousand sucres per dollar.

lines.text: People could swap their sucre notes at the central bank until about March 2001.
lines.say: People could swap their sucre notes at the central bank until about March two thousand one.

lines.text: One quirk: Ecuador still mints its own centavo coins, which circulate next to US coins. But it prints no paper money.
lines.say: One quirk: Ecuador still mints its own centavo coins, which circulate next to US coins. But it prints no paper money.

lines.text: So did it work? Here's Ecuador's annual inflation from World Bank data, 1996 through 2004.
lines.say: So did it work? Here's Ecuador's annual inflation from World Bank data, nineteen ninety-six through two thousand four.

lines.text: It climbed from about 24% in 1996 to the 96% peak in 2000.
lines.say: It climbed from about twenty-four percent in nineteen ninety-six to the ninety-six percent peak in two thousand.

lines.text: Then it fell fast: about 38% in 2001, 12.5% in 2002, and under 3% by 2004.
lines.say: Then it fell fast: about thirty-eight percent in two thousand one, twelve point five percent in two thousand two, and under three percent by two thousand four.

lines.text: And it has stayed low. In December 2025, Ecuador's annual inflation was 1.91%, according to its statistics agency, INEC.
lines.say: And it has stayed low. In December twenty twenty-five, Ecuador's annual inflation was one point nine one percent, according to its statistics agency, I N E C.

lines.text: Since then, the dollar has outlasted several changes of government in Ecuador.
lines.say: Since then, the dollar has outlasted several changes of government in Ecuador.

lines.text: Chapter three: the dollar club.
lines.say: Chapter three: the dollar club.

lines.text: Panama and Ecuador aren't the only members.
lines.say: Panama and Ecuador aren't the only members.

lines.text: El Salvador joined in 2001. Its Monetary Integration Law fixed the rate at 8.75 colones per dollar.
lines.say: El Salvador joined in two thousand one. Its Monetary Integration Law fixed the rate at eight point seven five colones per dollar.

lines.text: By the end of 2001, almost only dollars were circulating there.
lines.say: By the end of two thousand one, almost only dollars were circulating there.

lines.text: Then, in September 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make bitcoin legal tender, alongside the dollar.
lines.say: Then, in September twenty twenty-one, El Salvador became the first country to make bitcoin legal tender, alongside the dollar.

lines.text: Under that law, businesses generally had to accept bitcoin when a customer offered it.
lines.say: Under that law, businesses generally had to accept bitcoin when a customer offered it.

lines.text: In January 2025, after a $1.4 billion loan deal with the IMF, lawmakers amended the law. Accepting bitcoin became voluntary.
lines.say: In January twenty twenty-five, after a one point four billion dollar loan deal with the I M F, lawmakers amended the law. Accepting bitcoin became voluntary.

lines.text: Through all of it, the US dollar stayed El Salvador's everyday currency.
lines.say: Through all of it, the US dollar stayed El Salvador's everyday currency.

lines.text: Timor-Leste, in Southeast Asia, has used the dollar since 2000, when it was under UN administration. It added its own centavo coins in 2003.
lines.say: Timor-Leste, in Southeast Asia, has used the dollar since two thousand, when it was under UN administration. It added its own centavo coins in two thousand three.

lines.text: In the Pacific, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau use the dollar too, tied to their compacts with the US.
lines.say: In the Pacific, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau use the dollar too, tied to their compacts with the US.

lines.text: Zimbabwe is the messy case. Its official inflation hit 231 million percent in 2008.
lines.say: Zimbabwe is the messy case. Its official inflation hit two hundred thirty-one million percent in two thousand eight.

lines.text: In April 2009, it abandoned its own dollar and let people use foreign money, led by the US dollar.
lines.say: In April two thousand nine, it abandoned its own dollar and let people use foreign money, led by the US dollar.

lines.text: Zimbabwe brought back its own dollar in 2019, and that one struggled too.
lines.say: Zimbabwe brought back its own dollar in twenty nineteen, and that one struggled too.

lines.text: In April 2024, it launched a new gold-backed currency called the ZiG, while US dollars kept circulating.
lines.say: In April twenty twenty-four, it launched a new gold-backed currency called the Zig, while US dollars kept circulating.

lines.text: And in February 2026, its central bank reportedly dropped a 2030 deadline for ending the multicurrency system.
lines.say: And in February twenty twenty-six, its central bank reportedly dropped a twenty thirty deadline for ending the multicurrency system.

lines.text: So the dollar club is bigger than most people think.
lines.say: So the dollar club is bigger than most people think.

lines.text: Chapter four: the trade-offs.
lines.say: Chapter four: the trade-offs.

lines.text: Every dollarized country makes a trade. It gets low inflation, no risk of its own currency crashing, and instant credibility. In return, it gives up its own interest rates, the power to devalue, and a backstop for its banks.
lines.say: Every dollarized country makes a trade. It gets low inflation, no risk of its own currency crashing, and instant credibility. In return, it gives up its own interest rates, the power to devalue, and a backstop for its banks.

lines.text: The biggest gain is the one we just charted. Ecuador went from 96.1% inflation in 2000 to 2.7% by 2004.
lines.say: The biggest gain is the one we just charted. Ecuador went from ninety-six point one percent inflation in two thousand to two point seven percent by two thousand four.

lines.text: Second, credibility. People and lenders can plan in a currency the local government can't print, which economists say can make long-term loans easier to get.
lines.say: Second, credibility. People and lenders can plan in a currency the local government can't print, which economists say can make long-term loans easier to get.

lines.text: Now the costs. First, there's no lender of last resort. A normal central bank can create money to rescue banks in a panic.
lines.say: Now the costs. First, there's no lender of last resort. A normal central bank can create money to rescue banks in a panic.

lines.text: Ecuador's central bank still exists, but it can't print dollars. In a bank run, it only has the dollars it already holds.
lines.say: Ecuador's central bank still exists, but it can't print dollars. In a bank run, it only has the dollars it already holds.

lines.text: Second, interest rates are effectively set in Washington. Whatever the Fed does, dollarized countries feel it.
lines.say: Second, interest rates are effectively set in Washington. Whatever the Fed does, dollarized countries feel it.

lines.text: In September 2026, for example, the Fed raised its target range to 3.75% to 4%. That decision was made for the US economy, not for Ecuador or Panama.
lines.say: In September twenty twenty-six, for example, the Fed raised its target range to three point seven five percent to four percent. That decision was made for the US economy, not for Ecuador or Panama.

lines.text: When US rates rise, borrowing costs tend to rise in dollarized countries too, whether their economies need it or not.
lines.say: When US rates rise, borrowing costs tend to rise in dollarized countries too, whether their economies need it or not.

lines.text: Third, no devaluing. When the dollar is strong, a country with its own currency can let it fall, which makes its exports cheaper abroad. Ecuador and Panama can't.
lines.say: Third, no devaluing. When the dollar is strong, a country with its own currency can let it fall, which makes its exports cheaper abroad. Ecuador and Panama can't.

lines.text: Mexico, for example, has its own peso, so its exchange rate can move. A dollarized country has to adjust through wages and prices instead, which is slower and more painful.
lines.say: Mexico, for example, has its own peso, so its exchange rate can move. A dollarized country has to adjust through wages and prices instead, which is slower and more painful.

lines.text: Fourth, lost seigniorage. That's the profit a government makes by issuing money that costs less to produce than it's worth.
lines.say: Fourth, lost seigniorage. That's the profit a government makes by issuing money that costs less to produce than it's worth.

lines.text: When a country uses dollars, that profit goes to the United States instead.
lines.say: When a country uses dollars, that profit goes to the United States instead.

lines.text: Which brings us to Argentina, the biggest country where this debate has played out.
lines.say: Which brings us to Argentina, the biggest country where this debate has played out.

lines.text: In the 2023 presidential campaign, Javier Milei proposed dollarizing Argentina's economy.
lines.say: In the twenty twenty-three presidential campaign, Javier Milei proposed dollarizing Argentina's economy.

lines.text: As president, he said in February 2024 that dollarization is the final step of a long process, not a short-term goal, according to the Buenos Aires Times.
lines.say: As president, he said in February twenty twenty-four that dollarization is the final step of a long process, not a short-term goal, according to the Buenos Aires Times.

lines.text: As of late 2026, Argentina still uses the peso, with exchange-rate bands adjusted monthly for inflation since January 2026.
lines.say: As of late twenty twenty-six, Argentina still uses the peso, with exchange-rate bands adjusted monthly for inflation since January twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Supporters say dollarizing would end high inflation for good and build trust. Critics say Argentina would need a huge pile of dollars to do it, and it would lose key policy tools.
lines.say: Supporters say dollarizing would end high inflation for good and build trust. Critics say Argentina would need a huge pile of dollars to do it, and it would lose key policy tools.

lines.text: Chapter five: your wallet.
lines.say: Chapter five: your wallet.

lines.text: So what does all this mean for normal people?
lines.say: So what does all this mean for normal people?

lines.text: Start with savings. In a dollarized country, savings can't be wiped out by a currency collapse like Ecuador's in 1999.
lines.say: Start with savings. In a dollarized country, savings can't be wiped out by a currency collapse like Ecuador's in nineteen ninety-nine.

lines.text: Banks can still get into trouble, though. Using dollars protects the currency, not every individual bank.
lines.say: Banks can still get into trouble, though. Using dollars protects the currency, not every individual bank.

lines.text: Next, prices. Because prices are in dollars, they don't jump just because a local currency slides.
lines.say: Next, prices. Because prices are in dollars, they don't jump just because a local currency slides.

lines.text: Third, remittances, the money migrants send home.
lines.say: Third, remittances, the money migrants send home.

lines.text: In 2025, Ecuador received a record $7.73 billion in remittances, according to its central bank.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, Ecuador received a record seven point seven three billion dollars in remittances, according to its central bank.

lines.text: That's up 18.2% from $6.54 billion in 2024.
lines.say: That's up eighteen point two percent from six point five four billion dollars in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: About 78% of it, roughly $6 billion, came from the United States.
lines.say: About seventy-eight percent of it, roughly six billion dollars, came from the United States.

lines.text: And there's no currency conversion at the end. A dollar sent from New Jersey arrives in Quito as a dollar, minus any transfer fees.
lines.say: And there's no currency conversion at the end. A dollar sent from New Jersey arrives in Quito as a dollar, minus any transfer fees.

lines.text: Finally, travel. For American tourists in Ecuador, Panama, or El Salvador, there's no money to exchange.
lines.say: Finally, travel. For American tourists in Ecuador, Panama, or El Salvador, there's no money to exchange.

lines.text: And here's the twist for Americans: every Fed decision you hear about also lands in Quito, Panama City, and San Salvador.
lines.say: And here's the twist for Americans: every Fed decision you hear about also lands in Quito, Panama City, and San Salvador.

lines.text: Chapter six: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Panama has used the dollar since 1904, apart from one week of its own banknotes in 1941.
lines.say: Panama has used the dollar since nineteen oh four, apart from one week of its own banknotes in nineteen forty-one.

lines.text: Ecuador adopted it in 2000, after its banks froze and the sucre fell to 25,000 per dollar.
lines.say: Ecuador adopted it in two thousand, after its banks froze and the sucre fell to twenty-five thousand per dollar.

lines.text: Inflation dropped from 96.1% in 2000 to 2.7% by 2004.
lines.say: Inflation dropped from ninety-six point one percent in two thousand to two point seven percent by two thousand four.

lines.text: The deal trades low inflation and credibility for a loss of control: no own interest rates, no devaluing, and no printing press.
lines.say: The deal trades low inflation and credibility for a loss of control: no own interest rates, no devaluing, and no printing press.

lines.text: And that means the Fed's decisions, like its September 2026 hike, reach far beyond the United States.
lines.say: And that means the Fed's decisions, like its September twenty twenty-six hike, reach far beyond the United States.

lines.text: So the next time you hold a dollar bill, remember it's also everyday money in Quito, Panama City, and San Salvador.
lines.say: So the next time you hold a dollar bill, remember it's also everyday money in Quito, Panama City, and San Salvador.

post.yt_desc:
Ecuador killed its own currency in 2000 at 25,000 sucres per dollar, and Panama has used the US dollar since 1904. This video explains dollarization in plain words: Panama's 1904 deal and its seven-day banknotes of 1941, Ecuador's 1998-2000 crisis (bank freeze, a collapsing sucre, 96.1% inflation in 2000), and what happened next. We cover El Salvador and its bitcoin law, Zimbabwe, Timor-Leste and the Pacific, the real trade-offs (low inflation versus no lender of last resort and rates set by the Fed), Argentina's debate, and what it means for savings, prices and remittances.

Sources: World Bank, World Development Indicators, inflation, consumer prices (Ecuador, 1996-2004); IMF (Ecuador, 2000); INEC via Ecuador Ministry of Finance (December 2025 inflation); Banco Central del Ecuador remittance data for 2025 via El Comercio (2026); U.S. State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States (Panama, 1904); Christian Science Monitor (August 2000); El Comercio (Ecuador); Federal Reserve FOMC statement (September 16, 2026); Buenos Aires Times (February 2024); Cointelegraph (January 2025); Nehanda Radio (February 2026).

News and education, not financial advice.
